questions.q: You have a 2 a.m. backup and no WAL archive. A mistaken DELETE happens at 3:02 p.m. What is the most you can recover?
questions.hint: No transaction between 2 a.m. and 3:02 p.m. is stored anywhere.

options.text: The 2 a.m. state; about 13 hours of later data are lost
options.why: Without WAL you can only go back to the moment of the backup; the writes in between are stored nowhere.

options.text: The state at exactly 3:01 p.m.
options.why: That needs a WAL archive, which you don't have here.

options.text: Nothing; a DELETE can't be undone
options.why: The 2 a.m. backup at least gets you back to that moment.

options.text: The deleted orders can be brought back from the replica
options.why: The DELETE reached the replica instantly too.

questions.q: Which of these are part of the 3-2-1 rule?
questions.hint: Think about what each of the three numbers means.

options.text: Three copies in total (including the original)
options.why: One original and two backup copies, so that losing one still leaves others.

options.text: Two kinds of medium or location (say disk and object storage)
options.why: One kind of failure shouldn't take all the copies at once.

options.text: One copy at another location or region
options.why: It survives a fire, a flood or the loss of a whole region.

options.text: All three copies in three directories of the same server
options.why: If the server dies, all three go. That is really one copy.

questions.q: What is wrong with this restore command?
questions.code:
# on the production server, with the DB running
pgbackrest --stanza=main restore \
  --type=time --target='2026-11-20 15:01:00' \
  --target-action=promote
questions.hint: Which server, and what is missing from the time?

options.text: It restores over the live production DB, and the target time has no timezone
options.why: Restoring over a live DB wipes all current data, and a time without a timezone can land on the wrong moment.

options.text: Using `--target-action=promote` is wrong
options.why: promote is right; it brings the DB up once the target is reached.

options.text: pgBackRest doesn't support PITR
options.why: It does; `--type=time` is for exactly this.

options.text: There is nothing wrong
options.why: There are problems: the live DB and the timezone.

questions.q: The weekly restore drill succeeds, but the restore took 110 minutes. The business RTO is 60 minutes. What should you do?
questions.hint: What is the real result of the drill?

options.text: Treat the gap as a problem and find ways to restore faster (incremental backups, faster disks, splitting the DB)
options.why: This is exactly what a drill is worth: finding out before disaster that you miss the target.

options.text: "It restored", so all is well
options.why: The RTO target was missed. On the day of an incident the business would be down for 110 minutes.

options.text: Change the RTO figure on paper to 120 minutes
options.why: The business need doesn't change on paper; the system has to change.

options.text: Stop the drills so the bad numbers stop appearing
options.why: Hide the number and the first time you learn it is on the day of the disaster.

questions.q: Which signs in a runbook are dangerous?
questions.hint: Someone half asleep is reading it at 3 a.m.

options.text: The last drill was six months ago, and a command has been renamed since
options.why: An old runbook tells you to run the wrong command, and its time estimate is wrong too.

options.text: The steps are long paragraphs with no commands, just "restore properly"
options.why: Vague instructions can't be followed under stress.

options.text: It doesn't say when to stop and whom to call
options.why: If you don't know what to do when stuck, you lose time.

options.text: Each step has its expected result written next to it
options.why: That is a good quality; it stops you going down a wrong path.

questions.q: PITR on the scratch server brought back the 1,200,000 deleted orders. Production has 300 new orders since the mistake. How do you bring the lost ones back?
questions.hint: The 300 new orders exist only in production.

options.text: Load the restored rows into a staging table, then INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING into orders
options.why: Today's 300 orders stay untouched, and only the missing rows are added.

options.text: Swap the scratch server in as the new production DB
options.why: The scratch copy stops at the target time, so the 300 newer orders would vanish.

options.text: Run TRUNCATE on orders, then load the whole restored table
options.why: That destroys the 300 new orders for the sake of a cleaner load.

options.text: INSERT the restored rows straight into orders
options.why: Any overlapping id raises a duplicate-key error and the load stops halfway.

questions.q: You must rerun 3000 failed jobs, and the handler has no guard. What is the first thing to do?
questions.hint: What must be fixed before running anything?

options.text: Make the handler idempotent and count with a dry run
options.why: Without a guard, partly done jobs will double. Make it safe first, count, then run slowly.

options.text: Dispatch everything at once, so it finishes quickly
options.why: You risk both double processing and overloading the system.

options.text: Increase the number of workers tenfold
options.why: It is faster, but the doubling and the load both get worse.

options.text: Run it at night when nobody is looking
options.why: The risk doesn't shrink with the clock; a double credit is just as double at night.

questions.q: The replay command crashes at event 2500. A checkpoint is saved at the end of each batch (100 events). What happens when you run it again?
questions.hint: Where is the last saved checkpoint?

options.text: It resumes from 2400; events 2401-2500 may run again, so the handler must be idempotent
options.why: The checkpoint is saved at the end of a batch. The batch that crashed runs again, and the guard makes that harmless.

options.text: From the very start (1)
options.why: The checkpoint exists to avoid exactly this.

options.text: From 2501, and nothing repeats
options.why: No checkpoint was saved up to 2500; it only goes up to 2400.

options.text: Nothing will run until you delete the checkpoint by hand
options.why: You don't need to delete anything; the command reads the checkpoint itself.

questions.q: What is the most dangerous flaw in this command?
questions.hint: Where are the limit, the rehearsal and the bookmark?

options.text: No throttle, no dry run, no checkpoint: everything is dispatched at once, and a crash means starting over
options.why: Three of the four safeguards are missing, and we don't know whether the handler is idempotent either.

options.text: The name `all()` is poor
options.why: The name doesn't matter; the problem is the behavior.

options.text: It should be `array_map` instead of `foreach`
options.why: The kind of loop isn't the problem.

options.text: No problem; it is short code, so it is safe
options.why: Short code can do great damage; the lack of safeguards is the problem.

questions.q: Which of these are safe ways to handle a replay?
questions.hint: Think about money, email and outside APIs.

options.text: Money writes in one transaction with a UNIQUE processed_event guard
options.why: On a second arrival, 0 rows are inserted and nothing happens.

options.text: Queueing one receipt row per event (UNIQUE event_id) and emailing from that table
options.why: A sent email can't be recalled. One row per event means one email, and a receipt the first attempt missed still gets queued.

options.text: Sending the original transaction's Idempotency-Key again to an outside API
options.why: The other side recognizes the same work and does it only once.

options.text: Generating a fresh Idempotency-Key for every call
options.why: A new key means new work on the other side, so you get a double charge.

questions.q: During a replay, DB CPU goes above 80% and user pages become slow. What should you do?

options.text: Lower the replay rate or pause it; thanks to the checkpoint you can resume from there later
options.why: Normal service comes first. With the checkpoint and the idempotent guard, stopping is safe.

options.text: Raise the rate even more to finish sooner
options.why: The load grows further, and so does the users' pain.

options.text: Drop every index in the database
options.why: That would make everything slower.

options.text: Stop the replay and delete the failed events
options.why: Once the events are deleted, the lost work can't be recovered.

questions.q: Event 1731 was credited, then failed before its receipt. The replay has a processed_event guard and a "skip email during replay" flag. What goes wrong?
questions.hint: What does the flag skip besides a duplicate?

options.text: The customer is credited correctly but never gets a receipt
options.why: The guard skips the credit (right), but the flag also skips the one receipt that was never sent.

options.text: The customer is credited twice
options.why: The processed_event guard stops a second credit.

options.text: The customer gets two receipts
options.why: The flag stops all emails in a replay, so none is sent at all.

options.text: Nothing: the flag handles every case
options.why: It handles duplicates but loses missed receipts. A receipt row per event handles both.

questions.q: A bad deploy wrote the wrong `fee_minor` on 1200 payments. What is the best first step?
questions.hint: What must you count and write down before fixing anything?

options.text: Find the affected rows with a narrow condition, do a dry run, agree the count in review, then run an audited script
options.why: Count, show, approve, then change. Every step is a chance to catch a mistake.

options.text: Run `UPDATE payment SET fee_minor = 1000` in the console
options.why: There is no condition, so every row changes, and no log is kept.

options.text: Restore the whole DB from a backup
options.why: You would lose the valid transactions that came after the mistake. A very heavy path.

options.text: Do nothing; the mistakes are small
options.why: A wrong fee affects the customer's money, and the books won't balance.

questions.q: In the ledger, $5,000 was posted as a deposit instead of $500. What do you do?

options.text: Write a reversing entry for the wrong transaction and post a new correct one for $500
options.why: History stays intact and debit = credit holds. The auditor gets the whole story.

options.text: `UPDATE ledger_entry SET amount_minor = 50000` ($500)
options.why: Changing a ledger entry is forbidden, and changing one side breaks the balance between the two sides.

options.text: Delete the wrong entry and insert a new one
options.why: Deleting erases history; an audit could prove nothing.

options.text: Reduce the wallet's balance column by $4,500
options.why: The balance is the result of the entries; changing it directly creates a mismatch with them.

questions.q: What risk is there in this data-fix SQL?
questions.hint: Where are the time window, the reason and the log?

options.text: Genuinely canceled orders will change too, and the old values are written nowhere
options.why: The condition is far too broad, and there is no log or count check.

options.text: `SET` should be written before `WHERE`
options.why: That is the normal SQL structure; the problem is how broad the condition is.

options.text: `UPDATE` never runs in production
options.why: It does, but with a documented, narrow condition.

options.text: There is no risk
options.why: There is; a one-liner like this was the root cause of the incident.

questions.q: Which are features of a good data-fix script?
questions.hint: Think of three moments: before, during and after the run.

options.text: It stops if the expected count doesn't match
options.why: A wrong condition is caught before it runs.

options.text: It writes each row's before and after values to a log
options.why: The basis for audit and, if needed, reversing it.

options.text: Running it again changes 0 rows
options.why: No double fix, and re-running after a crash is safe.

options.text: One person writes it and runs it straight in production without review
options.why: A second pair of eyes is the cheapest way to catch a wrong condition.

questions.q: The new release dropped the `phone` column and wrote data into a new `phone_e164` column, and now a bug is found. What is the safest path?
questions.hint: Can the old code run without the `phone` column?

options.text: Roll forward: deploy a small fix, plus an audited data fix for the bad data
options.why: The column is gone, so going back to the old code would break. Fixing ahead is safer.

options.text: Roll the code back, and think about the column later
options.why: The old code will fail writing to the dropped column, and create fresh trouble.

options.text: Restore the whole DB from backup
options.why: You would lose many valid transactions. It is a last resort, not a first move.

options.text: Do nothing and wait
options.why: The bug will keep piling up more bad data.

questions.q: FIX-1042 changed 2300 orders and turned out to be wrong. How do you undo it?
questions.hint: Where did the fix record each row's old value?

options.text: Update orders from `data_fix_log`, only for rows whose status still equals the logged new value
options.why: The log has every row's old value, and the guard leaves rows changed since untouched.

options.text: Restore the whole DB from last night's backup
options.why: You would lose every valid transaction since then. The log makes this unnecessary.

options.text: Run the fix script again
options.why: It finds 0 rows, because the condition no longer matches the fixed rows.

options.text: UPDATE orders SET status = 'canceled' WHERE status = 'paid'
options.why: That cancels every paid order, not just the 2300 the fix touched.
